prompt: An idle rented GPU still bills hourly.
explanation: True: a rented GPU bills the same hourly rate whether it is busy or idle, so unused time is waste.

prompt: What is GPU utilization?
explanation: Utilization measures how much of the GPU's capacity is actually doing useful work.

prompt: Low utilization makes cost per request ___.
explanation: You pay the same bill while doing less work, so each request costs more.

prompt: Which raises utilization?
explanation: Batching keeps the GPU busy by processing several requests at once.

prompt: What lifts utilization?
explanation: Batching packs the work; scaling in removes idle capacity. Extra idle replicas do the opposite.

prompt: Does each raise or lower unit cost?
explanation: Anything that leaves capacity unused raises cost per request.

prompt: A GPU is busy 20% of time. Utilization?
explanation: Busy share of time is the utilization, so 20%.

prompt: Rented GPU idle half the day. Cost per request?
explanation: You pay the same bill for less work, so each request costs more.

prompt: Hosted LLM APIs charge by the amount of text processed.
explanation: Providers bill per token, often quoted per million tokens, so longer prompts and answers cost more.

prompt: Hosted LLM APIs charge per ___.
explanation: Token counts, from the earlier deck on tokens, drive the price of each call.

prompt: Output tokens often cost ___ than input tokens.
explanation: Generating tokens one at a time is costlier than reading the prompt, so providers typically charge more for output.

prompt: Which cuts API spend?
explanation: Fewer tokens in means a smaller bill, so trim needless instructions.

prompt: Which reduce token spend?
explanation: Trimming, reusing, and capping all lower tokens billed.

prompt: Match the billing term.
explanation: Input is what you send, output is what the model writes, and both live within the context window.

prompt: Price is quoted per?
explanation: Rates are usually expressed per one million tokens so numbers stay readable.

prompt: Chatbot bills spiked from long system prompts. Fix?
explanation: Fewer input tokens means a smaller bill.

prompt: Self-hosting only beats an API above some traffic volume.
explanation: True: self-hosting only wins above a certain traffic volume; with low traffic a per-token API is often cheaper.

prompt: What is the break-even point?
explanation: Break-even is the traffic volume where self-hosting costs the same as paying an API.

prompt: Low steady traffic usually favors an ___.
explanation: With little traffic a dedicated GPU sits idle, so pay-per-use is cheaper.

prompt: Heavy steady traffic often favors?
explanation: A busy GPU spreads its fixed cost over many requests, beating per-token prices.

prompt: Which optimizations cut cost per request?
explanation: Each lets the same hardware serve more requests. Idle replicas only add cost.

prompt: Which option suits each workload?
explanation: Match cost structure to demand: variable pay for low use, fixed hardware for high use.

prompt: Order by rising traffic.
explanation: As traffic grows, the case for self-hosting improves.

prompt: Only 50 requests daily. Best choice?
explanation: Below break-even, a dedicated GPU sits idle, so pay-per-use is cheaper.

prompt: A phone can run a model without any internet connection.
explanation: Live translation on a plane works because the model lives on the device.

prompt: What is on-device inference?
explanation: On-device (edge) inference runs the model on the user's own phone, laptop, or gadget rather than a remote server.

prompt: On-device models keep data on the ___.
explanation: Nothing needs to be uploaded, which helps privacy.

prompt: Which is an on-device benefit?
explanation: No network round trip is needed, so it works without a connection.

prompt: Edge inference advantages include?
explanation: Local processing avoids uploads and network delay. Devices actually have limited RAM.

prompt: Match the place to its trait.
explanation: Each location trades power against privacy and speed.

prompt: Cloud or edge benefit?
explanation: Big models fit in the cloud; privacy and offline use favor the edge.

prompt: App must translate on a plane. Approach?
explanation: Running locally needs no network connection.

prompt: Phones have far less memory and power than servers.
explanation: A phone shares a few gigabytes with all apps and runs on a battery, unlike a data center GPU.

prompt: What limits phone models?
explanation: Devices have small memory, battery limits, and heat limits, so models must be lean.

prompt: Thermal throttling makes a hot phone run ___.
explanation: Heat makes the phone reduce its own speed to protect itself.

prompt: Which helps a model fit a phone?
explanation: Lower-precision weights shrink the file and memory footprint.

prompt: Which shrink models for devices?
explanation: Earlier decks' size-reduction tools all apply, while bigger batches don't.

prompt: Device concern or server concern?
explanation: Battery and heat matter locally; fleets of replicas are a server issue.

prompt: Why do phone apps prefer small models?
explanation: Big models simply do not fit in shared phone memory.

prompt: Model won't fit in phone memory. First fix?
explanation: Lower-precision weights shrink the memory footprint.

prompt: Many phones include chips built just for neural networks.
explanation: An NPU does the same math as a CPU but faster and with less battery drain.

prompt: Which chip in phones runs neural networks?
explanation: A neural processing unit is a chip specialized for running neural networks efficiently.

prompt: An NPU saves both speed and ___.
explanation: Specialized hardware does the same math using less energy.

prompt: Which runtime targets Apple devices?
explanation: Core ML is Apple's framework for running models on its devices, using its neural hardware.

prompt: Which are on-device chips?
explanation: Phones may run models on any of these three. A data center is a place, not a chip.

prompt: Match chip to trait.
explanation: Each chip is tuned differently; NPUs are best for neural nets.

prompt: Order by AI specialization.
explanation: General-purpose CPUs are least specialized, GPUs handle parallel math, and NPUs are built for neural networks.

prompt: Battery drains fast running a vision model. Try?
explanation: An NPU does the same neural math with less energy.

prompt: Hybrid apps use both local and cloud models.
explanation: True: a hybrid app answers locally when it can and falls back to a bigger cloud model for hard requests.

prompt: What is a hybrid setup?
explanation: Hybrid deployment splits work between the device and the cloud, playing to each one's strengths.

prompt: Hybrid apps may fall back to the ___.
explanation: When the local model is unsure, the request goes to a larger cloud model.

prompt: How do device models get updated?
explanation: New model files are delivered like other app data, so they need versioning and size care.

prompt: Hybrid trade-offs include?
explanation: More moving parts appear, and cloud fallback sends data off-device.

prompt: Match task to place.
explanation: Small, private, latency-critical tasks stay local; heavy generation goes to the cloud.

prompt: Order a hybrid request.
explanation: Attempt cheap local inference first, escalate when needed, then return the result.

prompt: Phone answers easy prompts, hard ones fail. Design?
explanation: Try local first and escalate hard requests to a bigger cloud model.

prompt: Optimizing can quietly break a model that worked before.
explanation: After quantizing, a model might still run yet misread rare inputs. You only notice by checking.

prompt: What is a regression?
explanation: A regression is something that used to work correctly and now does not, such as lower accuracy after an optimization.

prompt: Regression testing compares against a ___.
explanation: You compare the optimized model against the original model's results.

prompt: When should you regression-test?
explanation: Every optimization can change outputs, so check right after each change.

prompt: Which need a baseline?
explanation: Any metric you want to protect needs a known starting value to compare against.

prompt: Match the term.
explanation: A tolerance says how much loss is acceptable before you reject the change.

prompt: Order a regression check.
explanation: Record what good looks like, apply the change, rerun, and compare against the baseline.

prompt: Quality fell after optimizing. Name for this?
explanation: Something that used to work well and now does not is a regression.

prompt: A fixed set of test inputs makes comparisons fair.
explanation: Running the same 500 questions before and after an optimization shows exactly what changed.

prompt: What is a golden set?
explanation: A golden set is a curated collection of inputs with known good outputs, reused for every comparison.

prompt: A golden set should cover ___ cases.
explanation: Include tricky and rare inputs, since optimizations often hurt those first.

prompt: Why keep a golden set fixed?
explanation: Changing tests between runs makes before-and-after numbers meaningless.

prompt: Good golden set traits?
explanation: It should mirror real use and be stable so results are comparable.

prompt: Good or bad golden set?
options: Real user samples↔Good|Only easy cases↔Bad|Rare inputs too↔Good|Changing daily↔Bad
explanation: Realistic, stable, and hard enough to catch problems is the goal.

prompt: What might a golden set hold?
explanation: Pairs of inputs and known-good outputs let you score results automatically.

prompt: Test questions changed between runs. Problem?
explanation: Before-and-after numbers only mean something on the same fixed test set.

prompt: Average latency can hide slow outliers.
explanation: True: averages hide a slow tail; a metric like p99 shows the slowest requests.

prompt: The ___ latency exposes slow outliers.
explanation: p99 is the time within which 99% of requests finish, so it exposes the slowest tail.

prompt: Compare p95 latency, not just the ___.
explanation: Averages hide the slow tail that frustrates real users.

prompt: Accuracy fell 3 points. Tolerance is 1. Ship?
explanation: The drop exceeds the tolerance you set, so the change fails the check.

prompt: Which should you compare after optimizing?
explanation: Quality, speed, and resources are the three things optimization trades.

prompt: Match each metric to what it measures.
explanation: Each metric watches a different side of the trade-off.

prompt: Order by strictness.
explanation: Higher percentiles reach further into the slow tail, so p99 is the strictest of the three.

prompt: Average latency looks fine, users complain. Check?
explanation: p99 exposes the slow tail that averages hide.

prompt: Models can be tested on live traffic.
explanation: Sending a small share of users to the optimized model limits damage if something is wrong.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
explanation: A canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new model first, so problems show up before everyone is affected. A shadow test is safer still: the new model sees copies of real requests, but its answers are never shown.

prompt: Shadow testing runs the new model ___ users.
explanation: The new model gets copies of real requests, but its answers are only logged, not shown.

prompt: Which test risks no users?
explanation: Shadow answers are never shown, so users cannot be harmed.

prompt: Safe release steps include?
explanation: Layered gradual checks plus an easy way back reduce risk.

prompt: Which sees users?
explanation: Only canary and full rollouts show answers to real users.

prompt: Order a safe rollout.
explanation: Move from least to most exposure, checking at each stage.

prompt: Want zero user risk testing a new model. Use?
explanation: Shadow answers are logged but never shown to users.

prompt: You cannot fix a slowdown until you know its cause.
explanation: Guessing wastes time. If memory is the limit, faster math changes nothing.

prompt: What comes first in optimizing?
explanation: Measure where time, memory, or money is going, so you spend effort on the real limit.

prompt: The ___ is the part limiting overall speed.
explanation: Speeding up anything other than the bottleneck barely helps.

prompt: Memory full, speed fine. Bottleneck?
explanation: The scarce resource is what to shrink, for example with quantization.

prompt: Which metrics reveal bottlenecks?
explanation: Profiling from earlier decks shows where resources go.

prompt: Match symptom to limit.
options: Out of memory↔Memory|Idle GPU↔Batching gap|High p99↔Queueing
explanation: Symptoms point to the resource actually causing trouble.

prompt: Order the first steps.
explanation: Know the target, gather data, locate the limit, and only then choose a technique.

prompt: Slow app, unknown cause. First step?
explanation: Find the real bottleneck before choosing any fix.

prompt: Some optimizations are cheap and safe; others need retraining.
explanation: Turning on batching or caching is a config change. Distillation needs a whole new training run.

prompt: Which usually comes first?
explanation: Start with low-effort, low-risk steps such as caching, batching, or a faster runtime.

prompt: Try config changes before ___ the model.
explanation: Retraining costs time, compute, and risk, so it comes later.

prompt: Cheap fix or heavy fix?
explanation: Caching and batching are config changes; distillation and quantization-aware training need training runs.

prompt: Low-effort speedups include?
explanation: Distillation requires training a new model, so it is heavier.

prompt: Which carries least accuracy risk?
explanation: Exact caching returns the same answer, so quality is untouched.

prompt: Order by effort, lowest first.
explanation: Cache first, then post-training quantization, then heavy retraining approaches.

prompt: Slow chatbot, deadline tomorrow. Try first?
explanation: Cheap config wins come before anything that needs retraining.

prompt: Different goals call for different optimizations.
explanation: Cutting memory needs smaller weights, but raising throughput needs better batching.

prompt: Goal: shrink memory. Try?
explanation: Lower precision weights take less space, the direct fix for memory limits.

prompt: Goal: more requests per second?
explanation: Batching packs more requests into each pass, raising throughput.

prompt: Goal: lower first-token delay?
explanation: Skipping recomputation of a shared prompt beginning speeds the first token.

prompt: Match goal to technique.
explanation: Each technique targets one lever: size, call volume, or which model answers.

prompt: Which reduce cost per request?
explanation: They let the same hardware do more useful work.

prompt: Which goal does each serve?
explanation: Size reducers help memory; scheduling tricks raise throughput.

prompt: Weights won't fit the GPU. Try?
explanation: Lower-precision weights take less space; replicas and bigger batches don't shrink the model.

prompt: Stop optimizing once you meet your target.
explanation: True: once the target is met, extra tuning adds risk and complexity for little gain.

prompt: When should you stop optimizing?
explanation: Once the goal is met, extra work trades away accuracy or simplicity for little gain.

prompt: Optimization stops once you meet the ___.
explanation: A concrete target, like p95 under 500 ms, defines when you are done.

prompt: Which is a good target?
explanation: A measurable target lets you tell whether the effort worked.

prompt: What belongs in a target?
explanation: Set limits for speed, spend, and minimum quality together.

prompt: Match to constraint.
explanation: Together these define the acceptable region of trade-offs.

prompt: Order the loop.
explanation: Iterate until the measured result meets the target, then stop.

prompt: p95 already under target. Next move?
explanation: Once the target is met, more tuning adds risk for little gain.

prompt: Guessing at slowness often optimizes the wrong thing.
explanation: Teams sometimes rewrite model code while the real delay is in tokenizing or waiting in a queue.

prompt: Biggest pitfall in optimizing?
explanation: Without profiling you might spend weeks speeding up something that was never the bottleneck.

prompt: Always ___ before changing anything.
explanation: Profiling shows what is really slow.

prompt: Rewrite model, but queue is slow. Result?
explanation: Optimizing a non-bottleneck barely changes total time.

prompt: Which are signs of careless optimizing?
explanation: Working without data or goals is the classic trap.

prompt: Match pitfall to fix.
explanation: Each mistake has a simple counter that earlier decks introduced.

prompt: Good habit or pitfall?
explanation: Habits are measured and goal-driven; pitfalls skip measurement.

prompt: Team rewrote model code; no speedup. Missed?
explanation: Without profiling, effort can go to something that was never the bottleneck.

prompt: Benchmarks predict production only when they resemble real traffic.
explanation: True: results only transfer when the test resembles real traffic in length, mix, and volume.

prompt: What makes a benchmark misleading?
explanation: Results only transfer if your test resembles production traffic in length, mix, and volume.

prompt: Skipping ___ runs inflates first-call latency numbers.
explanation: The first calls include one-time setup, so throw them away before measuring.

prompt: Why repeat benchmark runs?
explanation: One run can be a fluke, so repeat and use percentiles.

prompt: Which improve benchmark trust?
explanation: Realism, warmup, and repetition make numbers reliable.

prompt: Sound or flawed benchmark step?
options: Warmup first↔Sound|Single run↔Flawed|Real prompts↔Sound|Tiny prompts only↔Flawed
explanation: Sound steps mimic production and remove noise.

prompt: Order a benchmark.
explanation: Warm up, measure, repeat for stability, and report a percentile.

prompt: Benchmark used tiny prompts; production slower. Why?
explanation: Tiny prompts do not resemble real traffic.

prompt: Good average scores can hide rare failures.
explanation: After quantization a chatbot may keep 99% accuracy overall but stumble on unusual numbers or languages.

prompt: Average accuracy can hide rare ___.
explanation: Average accuracy hides that small groups of unusual inputs can degrade much more.

prompt: Check accuracy per ___, not overall.
explanation: A slice is a subgroup, such as one language or input type.

prompt: Skipped testing after quantizing. Risk?
explanation: Outputs still look plausible while quality quietly falls.

prompt: Which slices deserve checks?
explanation: Unusual conditions break first, so test them on purpose.

prompt: Match risk to check.
options: Rare inputs↔Slice test|Overall drop↔Baseline test|Slow tail↔Percentile
explanation: Different failure modes need different checks.

prompt: Overall or slice check?
explanation: Slices zoom into subgroups; overall metrics blend them together.

prompt: Overall accuracy fine, users report failures. Check?
explanation: Rare subgroups can fail while the average looks fine.

prompt: Bigger batches raise throughput but can slow each request.
explanation: Waiting to fill a batch of 32 gives the GPU more work per pass, but the first request waits.

prompt: What do huge batches do?
explanation: Requests wait for the batch to fill and run, so individual response time grows.

prompt: Batching trades ___ for throughput.
explanation: You accept some waiting to serve more requests per second.

prompt: Chat apps should prefer?
explanation: Interactive users care about response time more than raw throughput.

prompt: Over-optimization pitfalls include?
explanation: Improving one number at the expense of others, or continuing after the goal, wastes effort.

prompt: Match each optimization to its cost.
explanation: Each optimization gives up something, so know the price.

prompt: Order by batch size.
explanation: Larger batches raise throughput and typically increase waiting time.

prompt: Live chat feels laggy at batch 128. Fix?
explanation: Smaller batches cut waiting time, trading away some throughput.
